newsitem.title: USA: Jury convicts Berrigan, other peace protesters.
newsitem.headline: Jury convicts Berrigan, other peace protesters.

text.p: Veteran peace activist Phillip Berrigan and five other people were convicted by a federal jury Wednesday of illegally damaging a U.S. Navy warship in a protest against nuclear weapons.
The 12-member U.S. District Court panel took less than three hours to find the members of the "Prince of Peace Ploughshares" guilty on charges of destruction of government property and conspiracy.

The group smashed equipment and spilled blood Feb. 26 on the bridge of the destroyer USS The Sullivans, which was under construction at Bath Iron Works, causing between $80,000 and $100,000 in damage.
Berrigan and the other defendents, who acted as their own attorneys, face up to 15 years in prison and fines of up to $500,000. No sentencing date has been set.

Judge Gene Carter Tuesday barred the group from arguing their actions were justified by the immorality of war and by international laws aimed at stopping the spread of nuclear weapons. The Sullivans is capable of carrying nuclear warheads.
The group protested Carter's ruling by refusing to participate actively in the hearing. Two supporters were also arrested Wednesday when they attempted to climb the courthouse with a banner.

"The defendents admitted they engaged in the conduct and urged the jury to consider their political and religious beliefs ... We urged the jury to consider the facts of the case," Assistant U.S. Attorney Helen Kesanjian.

Berrigan, 73, a former Roman Catholic priest, has been active in the peace movement since the Vietnam War era. He was arrested in the Bath shipyard in 1991, but a state court later dropped the trespass charge.

Convicted with Berrigan were defendents Stephen Kelley, 48, of New York, Susan Crane, 53, of Ukiah, Calif., Thomas Borbely, 56, of Worcester, Mass., Steven Baggarly, 31, of Norfolk, Va. and Mark Colville, 36, of New Haven, Conn.
